the progenesis is a conditional strategy in S. anguillae, which can be induced by high temperatures and limited food availability.
progenesis in the trematode S. anguillae was more likely to occur at high temperatures and when worms were encysted in gonads or body tissues of their fish hosts.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the trematode Stegodexamene Anguillae is a facultatively progenetic parasite, with a greater propensity to adopt this developmental strategy at higher temperatures.

higher temperatures and/or lower body condition in the second intermediate fish host can trigger a facultative life cycle truncation in trematodes, which may be a strategy for coping with low probability of transmission.

the trematode Stegodexamene (formerly Clinostomum) anguillae is a parasite of the fish second host, the bluegill Lepomis macrochirus, which can become progenetic (produce eggs without the definitive host) under certain circumstances, and that this is more likely to occur at higher water temperatures, in fish with low body condition, and when the worms are encysted in gonadal or body cavity tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the parasite life cycle may be truncated by the parasite itself in order to ensure transmission to the next life cycle stage.
the parasite can adjust to environmental cues to maximise its transmission success.
parasites can be very flexible in how they develop and reproduce.
